newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea reverses reform stance, analysts sceptical.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea reverses reform stance, analysts sceptical.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party and government officials have back-pedalled and vowed to pursue legislation implementing financial reforms, and a powerful business lobby on Friday threw its weight behind change.
Friday's developments capped several days of waffling by the ruling party and Finance Ministry officials about whether financial reform should be pursued this year.
On Thursday, the ruling New Korea Party, supported by a contingent of Finance Ministry officials, said the government should delay reforms.

The party said the government needed more time to review reform proposals, which address controversial issues such as central bank independence, conglomerates' participation in bank management and mergers and acquisitions of financial companies.

But everything had changed by Friday when the party said it had agreed with the Finance Ministry to push forward with financial reforms, now being drafted by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform.
"We decided not to ask the government to delay the legislation," a party official said by telephone.
He said Kim Zoong-wie, chairman of the party's policy committee, had "retreated from his earlier stance." But he did not say why.

His change of heart followed a pledge by Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik late on Thursday to try to enact financial reform by submitting implementing legislation to a special parliamentary session in June.
Separately, the powerful Federation of Korean Industries on Friday urged the government to speed up the adoption of reforms.
It said financial reforms would ease pressures on companies that have had trouble securing financing because of a wave of debt defaults by big companies.
The federation, representing the interests of big business, offered a 38-point proposal that would, among other things, ease rules on direct financing and overseas financing.

The presidential commission is due to meet on Saturday to draft the final proposals to be sent to President Kim Young-sam by the end of May. But a commission official said the panel would refine some sensitive proposals next week.
Still, analysts remained sceptical about the likelihood that crucial reforms would be implemented this year.
"The financial reform issue seems to have gone back to the starting point," said Lee Keunmo, head of research at ING Barings. "I doubt parliament's intention to pass the laws."
Analysts said lawmakers, concerned about votes, were unlikely to take up hot issues ahead of a presidential election in mid-December.
"Passage of the bill is unlikely to go smoothly as the country would be caught up in the election," said Park Kyung-suh, senior economist at the Korea Institute of Finance.

The government should have proceeded with financial reform when President Kim took power in 1993 and the public supported his reform efforts, they said. Kim's term expires next February. He is barred from seeking a second term.
"I believe the ruling party doesn't want to repeat the bad experience they faced trying to revise the labour law ahead of an election," Lee said.

South Korea backed away from a labour law rammed through parliament last December after workers responded with some of the worst protests and strikes in years. In January, the president agreed to a watered-down version of the law.
